subject: History
topic: Land revenue systems — Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari, Mahalwari
description: Colonial land revenue systems: Permanent Settlement/Zamindari (1793, Cornwallis), Ryotwari (Thomas Munro, Madras/Bombay), Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie 1822, North India) — who pays, who owns, consequences for peasantry.

questions.stem: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 was introduced by Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. Under this system, revenue was to be paid by:

options.option_text: Zamindars, who became permanent proprietors of land in exchange for fixed annual payments
Individual cultivators (ryots) paying revenue directly to the colonial government
Village communities collectively, with the headman responsible for the payment
Local merchants who leased land from the government and sub-leased to farmers

questions.explanation: PERMANENT SETTLEMENT 1793: introduced by Lord Cornwallis (Governor-General). KEY FEATURES: (1) Zamindars recognised as PERMANENT PROPRIETORS (owners) of land. (2) Revenue fixed PERMANENTLY at 10/11ths of their collections — the British got a guaranteed revenue. (3) If zamindars failed to pay on the due date (Sunset Law/Suryast Law), their estate would be auctioned. AREAS: Bengal, Bihar, Orissa + some parts of Madras (northern districts). IMPACT ON ZAMINDARS: made them into landlords; they prospered when land values rose but revenue was fixed. IMPACT ON PEASANTS: peasants lost occupancy rights; rack-renting (charging high rents), eviction became common — zamindars collected as much as they could but paid only the fixed amount to British. THEORETICAL JUSTIFICATION: Philip Francis and Charles Cornwallis believed zamindars = English gentry → would invest in agriculture. REALITY: many zamindars became absentee landlords. PYQ FREQUENCY: Permanent Settlement details in SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims, IBPS PO History GA — very commonly asked.

questions.stem: The Ryotwari System, introduced in the Madras and Bombay Presidencies, is most associated with:

options.option_text: Thomas Munro — he advocated direct settlement with individual cultivating peasants (ryots)
Lord Cornwallis — he introduced the Permanent Settlement with zamindars in Bengal
Holt Mackenzie — he proposed the Mahalwari System for North-Western Provinces in 1822
Lord Wellesley — he is known for the Subsidiary Alliance System, not land revenue

questions.explanation: RYOTWARI SYSTEM: introduced by Thomas Munro and Alexander Read in Madras Presidency; later extended to Bombay by Mountstuart Elphinstone. 'Ryot' = peasant cultivator (from Arabic ra'iyya = subject/tenant). KEY FEATURES: (1) Direct settlement between the government and each INDIVIDUAL CULTIVATING PEASANT (ryot). (2) No intermediary zamindar. (3) Revenue assessed periodically (not permanent) — government could revise rates. (4) Peasant recognised as the owner of land AS LONG AS they paid the revenue. COVERAGE: Madras (~51% of Indian territory under Ryotwari eventually), Bombay Presidency, Sind, Berar, Assam, Coorg. ASSESSMENT: government set revenue at 45-55% of gross produce — very high. ADVANTAGE OVER ZAMINDARI: no intermediate exploiting class. DISADVANTAGE: high revenue demand, periodic reassessment created uncertainty; land mortgages and debt bondage became widespread. PYQ FREQUENCY: Ryotwari = Thomas Munro in SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims, IBPS PO, state PSC History — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The Mahalwari System introduced in North-Western Provinces differed from both Zamindari and Ryotwari primarily in that revenue was collected from:

options.option_text: Village communities (mahals) collectively, with the headman or landlords jointly responsible
Individual cultivators only, with the government bypassing the village structure entirely
Zamindars who owned entire regions and paid a fixed rent regardless of crop yield
Local merchants and moneylenders who financed the peasants and recovered revenue indirectly

questions.explanation: MAHALWARI SYSTEM: introduced by Holt Mackenzie (1822), later revised by R. M. Bird. 'Mahal' = an estate or village (from Arabic). KEY FEATURES: (1) Settlement with the VILLAGE COMMUNITY (mahal) as a whole, not individual peasants or zamindars. (2) The VILLAGE HEADMAN or collective of village elders responsible for paying the government revenue. (3) Individual cultivators owned their plots but the JOINT RESPONSIBILITY of the village guaranteed payment. (4) Revenue periodically revised. COVERAGE: North-Western Provinces (modern UP), Punjab, parts of Central India. COMPARISON: ZAMINDARI = one powerful landlord pays. RYOTWARI = each cultivator pays individually. MAHALWARI = village as a unit pays collectively. SIGNIFICANCE: reflected the traditional village structure of northern India more realistically. LAND ALIENATION: despite communal responsibility, heavy revenue demand led to debt and land alienation to moneylenders in Punjab (land alienation led to Punjab Land Alienation Act, 1900). PYQ FREQUENCY: Mahalwari = Holt Mackenzie = village community in SSC CGL, UPSC Prelims, state PSC — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The 'Sunset Clause' (Sunset Law/Suryast Law) under the Permanent Settlement meant that:

options.option_text: If a zamindar failed to pay revenue by sunset on the due date, his estate would be auctioned
After sunset, no agricultural activity was permitted on the zamindar's estate by law
Revenue rates would automatically sunset (expire) and decrease after 25 years of the settlement
Zamindars could only collect rent from their tenants before sunset to prevent night exploitation

questions.explanation: SURYAST (SUNSET) LAW: a strict enforcement clause of the Permanent Settlement. If a zamindar did not deposit the EXACT revenue amount by sunset on the deadline, their ZAMINDARI ESTATE would be SOLD by public auction the next day. PURPOSE: guaranteed the Company's revenue — no delays, no excuses. CONSEQUENCE: small zamindars who could not pay on time lost their estates; large zamindars and money-lenders bought up these estates at low prices → land concentration. BIDDING AT AUCTIONS: often fronted by Company's own servants or their relatives. BANARAS CASE STUDY: zamindars of Banaras lost estates; new urban-based zamindar class emerged. SIGNIFICANCE: shows how British revenue policy accelerated land concentration and impoverishment of old landed aristocracy. EXAM TRAP: don't confuse 'Sunset Law' with just 'setting a deadline' — it specifically means PUBLIC AUCTION if payment fails. UPSC ANGLE: Permanent Settlement created conditions for peasant distress that fuelled agrarian revolts (Indigo Revolt 1859-60, Pabna Agrarian League 1873). PYQ FREQUENCY: Sunset Law definition in UPSC Prelims, SSC CGL, state PSC 1× per 2-3 years.

questions.stem: The Deccan Riots of 1875 in Maharashtra are directly linked to which structural consequence of the Ryotwari System?

options.option_text: Peasant indebtedness to moneylenders — high revenue demand forced peasants to borrow at usurious rates
Zamindar oppression — zamindars evicted peasants who did not pay dues under the Ryotwari system
Government land grabbing — the British directly seized peasant lands for railway construction
Religious exploitation — the moneylenders imposed religious taxes on the Hindu peasant community

questions.explanation: DECCAN RIOTS 1875: uprising of peasants (mainly Kunbi and Mali communities) in Poona and Ahmednagar districts against moneylenders (mostly Marwari/Gujarati). Root Cause: Under Ryotwari, heavy revenue demands (British raised cotton cultivation revenues after American Civil War disrupted cotton supply → prices fell after 1865 → peasants stuck with debt). MONEYLENDER CYCLE: peasants borrowed from moneylenders at high interest → debts compounded → moneylenders seized land through fraudulent bonds → peasants rioted, snatching and burning debt documents. OUTCOME: Government appointed Deccan Riots Commission (1875) → led to Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879 (provided some debt relief and courts to adjudicate debt disputes). EXAM TRAP: Deccan Riots are in Ryotwari territory (Bombay Presidency) — NOT caused by zamindars (there were none under Ryotwari). Option B tries to mislead by introducing zamindars. RELATED UPSC ANGLE: Indigo Revolt 1859-60 (Bengal, Zamindari area); Champaran 1917; Bardoli Satyagraha 1928 — each reflects the specific land system's flaws. PYQ FREQUENCY: Deccan Riots cause in UPSC Prelims, state PSC History — 1× per 3-4 years.

questions.stem: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Drain of Wealth' theory argued that British land revenue policy was central to India's impoverishment. His key argument was that:

options.option_text: Surplus extracted via land revenue and trade was transferred to Britain, not reinvested in India
British land revenue policies were efficient but the zamindars spent too much on personal luxury
India's poverty was due to overpopulation and poor monsoons, not British extraction
Only cotton textile deindustrialisation caused poverty; land revenue had a minor role

questions.explanation: DADABHAI NAOROJI (1825-1917): called 'Grand Old Man of India'; first Indian elected to British Parliament (1892, Finsbury constituency). 'DRAIN OF WEALTH' THEORY: argued in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901) that ~£200 million/year was drained from India to Britain through: (1) HOME CHARGES: salaries of British officers, pensions paid from India's revenues. (2) TRADE SURPLUS: India exported more than it imported but the profits went to British companies. (3) LAND REVENUE surplus: extracted and remitted to London. He coined the term 'UNILATERAL TRANSFERS' — India exported goods without receiving value in return. R.C. DUTT (Romesh Chunder Dutt): 'Economic History of India' (1902) — documented how land revenue systems drained agricultural surplus. CONTRIBUTION: gave Indian National Congress a ECONOMIC critique of colonialism, not just political. 'INDIA PRODUCES WEALTH, ENGLAND ENJOYS IT' — his famous formulation. PYQ FREQUENCY: Drain of Wealth, Dadabhai Naoroji in UPSC Prelims, SSC CGL, state PSC — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: The Permanent Settlement has been called a 'mistake' by economic historians primarily because:

options.option_text: Fixing revenues permanently meant the government lost revenue as land values rose, while zamindars profited without investing in agricultural improvement
Zamindars paid too much revenue, making agriculture unprofitable and leading to mass abandonment of agricultural land across Bengal
It gave peasants too much security of tenure, reducing the government's ability to mobilise agricultural labour however
It created a class of small landowners who resisted British rule more effectively than large zamindars would have alone

questions.explanation: THE 'MISTAKE' DIAGNOSIS: two main critiques of Permanent Settlement by historians: CRITIQUE 1 (GOVERNMENT PERSPECTIVE): Revenue was fixed in PERPETUITY at 1793 rates. As land values rose with population and commercialisation (especially 19th century), zamindars collected increasing rents from tenants but paid the government the same fixed amount. The government LOST the 'unearned increment' (rising land values). James Mill and Utilitarian critics: permanent settlement was a fiscal mistake. CRITIQUE 2 (PEASANT PERSPECTIVE): Zamindars, not needing to improve land to increase income (land values rose anyway), had NO INCENTIVE to invest in irrigation, drainage, or technology. Sub-infeudation: zamindars created layers of rent-collecting intermediaries. Peasants at the bottom paid rising rents to multiple layers of intermediaries. BENGAL FAMINE 1943: often linked to long-term neglect of agricultural investment under the Zamindari system. COMPARE WITH RYOTWARI: Ryotwari allowed periodic revision of revenue → government captured rising land values → but burdened individual peasants with direct high assessments. UPSC ANGLE: Zamindari Abolition Acts (1950s) post-independence; Tenancy reform — Tebhaga Movement (1946 Bengal, 2/3 share for tenants). PYQ FREQUENCY: Permanent Settlement critique in UPSC Mains GS-1, state PSC, SSC CGL — conceptual angle 1× per 2-3 years.
